title: Potassium in Plants: What It Does and When Your Crop Needs It
metaTitle: Potassium in Plants: Role, Signs and When to Apply
metaDescription: Potassium in plants steers water, sugar and strong stems. See when palay, mais and gulay need it most, and why it is a regulator, not a building block.
excerpt: Potassium in plants is the regulator. It is not built into the plant body at all: it stays dissolved in the sap, where it opens and closes the leaf pores, moves sugar into the grain and keeps the stems firm. A crop short of it lodges, fills poorly and falls to disease. Here is what it does, when each crop needs it most and where it comes from.

heroImage.alt: Leaves with brown, scorched edges: potassium in plants running short

blocks.text:
Potassium opens and closes the stomata, the tiny pores on the leaves that let in air and let out water. So it decides how well a crop uses its water and how it stands a dry spell. It also switches on dozens of enzymes, and it pushes the sugar the leaves make down into the grain, the fruit and the root.

You see potassium most in the strength of a crop. It thickens cell walls and stems, so a well fed palay field stands up to wind and rain. It also helps the plant hold out against blast, sheath blight and other diseases, and it gives fruit their size, sweetness and color.
A regulator, not a building block

Potassium is a regulator. Unlike nitrogen and phosphorus it never becomes part of a protein, a gene or a wall. It stays free in the sap as a charged particle, steering water and switching enzymes on, and it can wash back out of old leaves in the rain.

Even so, crops take a lot of it, often as much as nitrogen. Most of it stays in the straw and the stalks, so returning the straw to the field gives much of it back. Burning the straw or taking it away for feed takes that potassium out of the farm.

blocks.caption: Potassium in short
rows: The old leaves, at the edges and tips

blocks.text:
Potassium moves freely, so the shortage starts on the older leaves. Their tips and edges turn yellow, then brown and dry, as if scorched, while the middle of the leaf stays green. In palay you often see it first as rusty brown spots on the lower leaves.

A crop short of potassium also lodges easily and catches more disease. See [potassium deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/potassium-deficiency) for the signs in each crop.
When potassium in plants is most critical

Potassium matters most when the crop builds its stem and then fills its grain or fruit. In palay that is panicle initiation through heading, when the stem has to carry the weight of the panicle and the sugar has to move into the grain. In fruit crops it is the weeks of fruit fill.

DAT means days after transplanting, DAS days after sowing in the field, and DAP days after planting. The days are the usual ones for a typical variety, so a long or short variety moves them a little. Timing potassium in plants to these windows gets more harvest from the same bags. Our guide to [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage) puts them together for a whole season.

Here is when each crop needs it most, from the anee.io stage book:

items: Palay, transplanted: Potassium after grain filling starts adds little. The straw already holds enough.
Yellow corn: Most potassium is taken up before tasselling. Later doses add little.
Sugarcane: Potassium in the last months adds little to cane weight.
Banana: Potassium after the bunch is full comes too late for it.

blocks.text: What keeps potassium from the crop

Sandy soil holds little potassium and loses it in heavy rain. Soils rich in clay can hold it tightly between their layers, and a soil heavy in calcium and magnesium, such as many limy or sodic soils, crowds potassium out at the roots. Too much ammonium or magnesium fertilizer also competes with it.

Removing the straw takes potassium off the farm every season. So the fields that get the full harvest of straw carried away need the most potassium back, and the fields where straw is returned need less.

Most potassium here is sold as muriate of potash, the cheapest potassium per kilogram. Sulfate of potash costs more but suits crops that dislike chloride, like tobacco and some vegetables. See our guide to [potash fertilizer](/blog/potash-fertilizer).

items: Muriate of potash (0 0 60): the usual potassium for palay and mais.
Sulfate of potash (0 0 50): potassium with sulfur, for chloride sensitive crops.
Complete fertilizer (14 14 14): potassium along with nitrogen and phosphorus.
Rice straw and wood ash: potassium returned to the field.

blocks.title: Too much potassium crowds out magnesium and calcium
blocks.text: Heavy potassium can push magnesium and calcium out at the roots and bring on their shortage, most of all on sandy soil. Balance it with what the soil test says.

blocks.title: Make sure potassium is there when the panicle forms
blocks.text: Put your fertilizers on your crop's calendar in anee.io and the [Coverage Planner](/features/residual-effect-calendar) shows, day by day, whether potassium reaches the stages that need it, and where it runs out. Free to start.

items.q: Is potassium the same as potash?
items.a: Potash is the fertilizer, potassium is the nutrient in it. Muriate of potash (0 0 60) is 60 percent potassium oxide.

items.q: When should I apply potassium to palay?
items.a: Part of it as basal, and a second dose at panicle initiation, about 35 to 45 days after transplanting. Potassium after grain filling starts adds little.
It helps a lot. Potassium thickens the stem walls, so the crop stands better in wind and rain. Too much nitrogen still makes a crop lodge, even with enough potassium.

items.q: Why is potassium called a regulator?
items.a: Because it is not built into the plant. It stays dissolved in the sap and controls water, enzymes and the movement of sugar.
